LanguageData.MX_Biography_Neiyu.stories.0.storyText:
It was sheer chance that Neiyu joined us. Around the campfire, people asked why a Milira so unlike the ones they knew had been traveling alone on the ground, and how she came to stay with us. She told us a few stories from the road.
She had always found the rimworlds a little too chaotic. On one small planet, civilization and savagery lived side by side. You could walk a few miles and go from order to violence. She'd helped a tribe gather enough food for a bitter winter and carried the Empire's beliefs to people who'd never heard of it. None of that seemed especially important to Neiyu. What mattered were all the different lives she'd glimpsed along the way.
Neiyu stood in the grass and felt the wind pass. It brushed her collar and stirred the pink flower pinned to it. She said the flower had been with her since she was born, and it hadn't wilted once. Whenever one journey ended, that ever-blooming flower would show her which way to go next.
These days, as a traveler, she went wherever she liked. Wherever the wind carried the petals, she followed. That's how she found us, the forty-second settlement on her journey. She said that if fate brought their paths together, she'd help anyone she met. Even if she might not be nearly as strong as she used to be.
"You've been to that many places," someone by the fire said. "What if you run into pigskins? Or tribals looking for a fight? They won't care who you are. If they're hungry enough, they might just jump you."
The speaker looked Neiyu up and down. "Especially since you don't seem to have a decent weapon on you."
The Raiment Blossom in her hand swayed in the firelight. "Even a rabbit bites if you corner it~ If it comes to it, I can run."
Neiyu smiled and looked up. "Apart from my friends up there, the ones who come from the same place as me, who could keep up?"
Everyone laughed. The fire was noisy again, and people went back to their food and idle chatter.
Skyfolk like Neiyu were rare to begin with, and she seemed unusual even among them. Maybe she was just a Milira who'd parted ways with her people to find a little freedom.
Come to think of it... weren't Milira supposed to be terrible cooks? How had she fed herself all the way here?
Neiyu listened to them talk, a faint smile rising to her lips.
She'd lost most of her power by now. Still, she had yet to meet anyone who could actually kill her.
LanguageData.MX_Biography_Neiyu.stories.1.storyText:
Neiyu had been in the colony for quite a while. Every so often she went into the nearby wilderness alone and brought back game for the butcher. By now, everyone was convinced this unusual Milira could take care of herself out there.
As for cooking… better leave that alone. Anyone who's heard of the Milira has probably heard enough about their cooking to be a little afraid.
Neiyu was used to it. She thought her cooking was perfectly fine, but if everyone insisted on laughing and ushering her out of the kitchen, she was happy to take the time off.
To Neiyu, the colonists were like lotus leaves on a pond, or the petals and leaves of a flower growing together. They argued sometimes, even over the smallest things. But the world outside was already such a mess. Compared with disputes that could get someone killed, a little bickering hardly seemed worth worrying about.
Neiyu always carried a little notebook. Ever since setting out, she'd used it to jot down anything she thought was worth remembering. Over the years, it had grown into a thick stack of pages.
Whenever someone pestered her for a story, Neiyu took out the notebook, closed her eyes, and opened it to a random page. Sometimes she looked wistful. Sometimes she nodded as if she'd just remembered something. And sometimes her eyes lit up and she kept everyone there for quite a while.
In time, listening to Neiyu became a habit. Life on a rimworld could be dull, and how often did a long-lived Milira from the sky come along to tell you about things you might never live to see?
One day, the smith spoke up as he hammered away at a piece of metal. “Miss Neiyu, what sort of weapon do you usually go for?”
Neiyu looked up. “What brought that on?”
The smith laughed. “You know how rough it gets out here. The colony's grown enough to kit everyone out with a decent weapon and some armor. Who knows if we'll live to see next month, or even tomorrow?”
He looked her up and down. “I've heard all sorts of stories about you Milira. You live in cities in the sky. In the old days, they say any one of you could hold your own against just about anything. But after spending some time with you…”
The smith scratched his head. “How come you seem kind of fragile?”
Someone nearby laughed. “Those wings are fast, sure, but they're hard to miss. They must be a weak spot. Want us to make you some armor?”
Neiyu looked down at herself. The other colonists had been getting new armor and weapons, while she still wore the same outfit, which looked like little more than cloth. If anyone looked like they needed protecting, it was her.
Neiyu thought about it, then gave a soft laugh. "Maybe it's because Milira almost never come down to the ground. People really don't know much about us. Though I'm not quite like my kin in the sky, either. Most of them have really impressive equip—"
Before she could finish, the alarm bell inside the room rang.
Clang!
The laughter stopped. Without a word, everyone set down what they were holding, grabbed their weapons and hurried outside to cover.
Neiyu stopped talking too. She took a moment to feel for movement in the distance. Pigskins. Not many. A patrol, probably.
Pigskins had always been quick to invade. Neiyu had told the colony about their tribes before. They kept growing in number and sent those they didn't need out to raid. With numbers on their side and weapons that were hardly primitive, some tribes had grown rich from raid after raid.
Maybe they'd spotted the colony's lights from a distance and crept over in the dark.
Neiyu gave it a moment's thought. Now that she thought about it... no one here really knew what she could do.
Behind cover, people raised their short guns. The pigskins kept coming. Just as someone was about to pull the trigger—
Fffwhip!
White light shot from behind them. It split in midair, one becoming two and two becoming three, then scattered into smaller arrows of light. Each found its own target and streaked into the distance.
The pigskins panicked. They'd never seen anything like it. Before they could react, the arrows were already there.
Thud. The arrows sank into flesh, and the pigskins fell almost as one.
For a moment the people behind cover forgot to fire. They turned instinctively. Neiyu was standing behind them, holding a huge longbow no one had seen her draw.
The bow looked like jade, or a crystal none of them had seen before. It gave off a soft blue and pink glow. A fine thread of pure light ran where the bowstring should have been.
Neiyu blinked at their expressions. "Don't worry. I can handle myself a little."
She paused, looking rather pleased with herself. "At least... I'm a pretty good shot. Hehe?"
With a flick of her hand, the great bow broke into pinpricks of light. They drew together and became a pink flower again, settling quietly into her hand.
Everyone stared for a long moment. Someone looked down at their own gun, then at the flower in Neiyu's hand. Was any of this supposed to make sense?
There was rather more to her story than they'd thought.
Not far away, crows had already landed beside the dead pigskins. Black beaks picked at the bodies. The wounds were deep and still bleeding.
Curiously, there was no trace of an arrowhead in any of them. It was as if the arrows that had taken their lives... had never existed.
LanguageData.MX_Biography_Neiyu.stories.2.storyText:
Neiyu had been here for several months. In that short time, she'd seen two lovers marry with everyone's blessing and a child born in the colony. The fields reached a little farther every week, and what had started as a handful of animals was beginning to crowd the pen.
She remembered when everyone sat together and made do with whatever simple food they had. Now there was enough for three meals a day, and they were beginning to taste good, too.
The houses grew more comfortable and the stores better stocked. Looking at the half-built houses and the ground set aside for new fields, people could see where the place was headed. They began to look forward to it.
There had been deaths, too. More people had joined the colony, some taken prisoner by Neiyu herself. Even after they'd surrendered and become colonists, she still saw a flicker of fear or hatred in their eyes whenever they met her.
"Why, though~" Neiyu sat high on the eaves, her legs dangling as she watched people go about their work below. She looked down and stroked the Raiment Blossom in her hands.
"I hurt him. I hurt his old friends too. But... we gave them a chance to live, and a place in a colony where they don't have to go hungry or cold."
Neiyu tipped her head. "We've always welcomed people with talent. They came to attack us first, though. Why do they still hate us after losing and being taken in?"
No one answered. She hadn't really been asking anyone. She gazed into the distance and began to hum a tune that had been part of her for as long as she could remember. She didn't know who'd first hummed it to her. It always came back when certain things were on her mind.
A past she had little wish to revisit slowly surfaced. Fragments came together into memories she'd forgotten.
——————————
“My God…”
This was the rimworld in an earlier age. Countless factions vied for its land: baseliners, xenotypes, tribes of every size, and outsiders with guns, armor, and strange technology.
The Milira of the sky were among them. Their sky cities hadn't been built yet. With strength far beyond most living beings, they fought across that chaotic land for a place where their people could survive.
Neiyu was still a child. Day after day she followed her teacher, learning how to swing a blade, how to dodge a blow, and how to kill an enemy.
Neiyu's teacher was one of the finest fighters and swordmasters among her people. Most Milira relied on powerful spells. She put her faith in the blade, using her own strength and skill to defeat anyone who stood in her way.
Four or five years after taking Neiyu in, her teacher finally agreed to bring her to a real battlefield.
“Teacher, I…” Neiyu stood before her, her voice faltering.
Her teacher said nothing and tossed her a long blade. Neiyu caught it instinctively. It was heavy, absurdly so for most people.
Her teacher reached out and ruffled her hair. “Don't be scared, little Yu. You've trained with me for years. You're one of the most talented kids I've ever taught.”
She pointed to the blade in Neiyu's hands. “Most of our weapons were taken from enemies. We're in no position to make many of our own. I looked a long time for that one. It should suit you best for now.”
Neiyu looked down at the weapon. The blade was nearly taller than she was. It looked comically out of place next to a child her size.
But they were Milira. It was as if the world had given them bodies and strength far beyond other forms of life from the day they were born. The blade was easier to carry than it looked. The halos above their heads were a source of pride and proof of what they were.
The Milira were proud in those days. There was little on that world that could truly threaten them.
Her teacher tapped the blade. “If it stops feeling right in your hands one day, you can give it back to me.”
She smiled. “By then, I expect you'll be able to stand on your own and win a little glory for yourself.”
Neiyu nodded solemnly. Her teacher turned to the horizon. “This is your first mission. I'll be with you the whole way. The leaders have their eye on a human granary. Our scouts say it's full of packaged food. All we have to do is take it. The transport crew will handle the rest.”
Her teacher sighed. “You know how hopeless we are at cooking. I barely survived the last meal Kaleli made.”
Neiyu couldn't help laughing. Some of the tension went out of her. Her teacher ruffled her hair again. “You'll be fine. I'll be right behind you.”
Young Neiyu gripped the long blade as if she'd just come to some momentous decision, then nodded hard. “Mm!”
The two flew toward the human settlement.
Humans… well, humans were good at plenty of things. Neiyu had read a lot about them.
They were relatively weak. They couldn't fly, they weren't very strong, and they didn't live long. Yet they were especially good at some peculiar things: cooking, building, making weapons that spat fire and metal.
Neiyu didn't really know why everyone kept fighting, but loyalty to her people carried her forward.
Buildings came into view in the distance. One enormous warehouse stood out in the middle of them. According to the scouts, that was their target.
There were fewer guards than expected. A few automated turrets stood around the settlement, but that kind of firepower posed little threat to the Milira of the day.
“Seventeen, eighteen.” Her teacher hovered beside her and counted the people below. “Eighteen humans in light armor. You can handle that.”
Neiyu tightened her grip on the blade. Her teacher looked at her again. “You know what I'm like, though. I'm still uneasy about sending you into your first battle.”
At the sight of her teacher's smile, Neiyu bristled. “I'll be fine! I've hunted packs of wolves before. Humans are just… bigger animals.”
“No,” her teacher said.
Neiyu blinked. Her teacher gave her a light tap on the head. “Don't think of them that way.”
“Huh?”
Her teacher looked down. The humans had spotted them. Most Milira at the time saw them, and other peoples, as little better than beasts: weak, short-lived, and so numerous they weren't worth respecting. Her teacher saw things differently.
“They're living people too,” she said calmly. “We fight because our people need us. They're defending their homes for the same reason.”
Neiyu stared at her and listened.
“We're the ones attacking today,” her teacher said without hesitation. “I think we have cause. Our people need food, so we have to fight for it. If we do nothing, our own go hungry. That doesn't give you leave to look down on everyone else alive on this world.”
She looked at Neiyu. “They're like us. They talk, have friends and families, and have their own civilization and language. We raise our swords for our own people. They'll pull the trigger for what they love.”
Her teacher patted her shoulder. “We just stand on different sides.”
Neiyu stood there for a long time. Everything she'd been taught as a child seemed to come apart and fit back together in a new order. She didn't quite understand, but she'd take her teacher's word over anyone else's. After all, that was her teacher.
“Go on.” Her teacher smiled. “I've got your back.”
“All right!” Neiyu beat her wings hard and hurtled toward the settlement.
The humans below spotted her almost at once. Alarms rang, turrets swiveled, and the lightly armored guards scrambled for their guns.
Neiyu tightened her grip on the blade. Her teacher's words were still running through her mind. “Humans are alive too… the way they think is probably much the same as ours. We just stand on different sides.”
…………
A little while later, Neiyu hurried back, beaming. “Teacher, teacher! Did I do it right?”
Her teacher looked down in silence. All eighteen humans lay trussed up tight. A few were struggling, some cursed, some looked terrified, and one was trying to chew through the rope.
Her teacher's eye twitched.
“It's what you said, isn't it?” Neiyu said, as if it were obvious. “Since humans are alive too, we can take what we came for and let them live. Their turrets can't hit me, and neither can their guns.”
Neiyu made a couple of quick gestures with her hand. “A few swipes, and down they went!”
Her teacher looked from Neiyu to the eighteen humans. She was quiet a long time. “…Maybe. Let's see about that food.”
“All right!”
The warehouse was even bigger than they'd expected. Heavy locks held the thick door shut. Her teacher plainly had no interest in asking the people cursing at them from the ground how to open it.
A sword rang from its sheath. A moment later, the wooden door splintered. The two stood looking at box after box of packaged food, stacked all the way through the warehouse.
The processed food would keep for a long time. With her people short of food, it was a valuable haul. Her teacher nodded in satisfaction. “Good. This will do.”
Neiyu grinned. Her first mission had gone well, and for the moment that was all that mattered. She ran up to the stacks and pulled out a packet. As soon as her teacher gave her permission, she tore it open and stuffed a bite into her mouth. Her eyes lit up.
“It's so good! Teacher, what is this? I've never tasted anything this good!”
Her teacher read the packet: Nutrition Paste Flavor Crispy Noodles.
Her teacher went quiet, then gave a dry laugh. “…As long as you like it.”
A piercing laugh came from outside the warehouse. “Ha ha ha ha ha! Worst choice you ever made!” It came from one of the men on the ground. His face was twisted with excitement and hate.
“Goodbye, sky elves.” With that, his body burst into flames.
The other prisoners stared. Alarm spread across their faces. Clearly, some of them had no idea what was about to happen.
The fire raced toward the warehouse along a barely visible trail on the ground. Her teacher's face changed. “No! Get out!”
She grabbed Neiyu before the girl could react, spread her wings, and shot into the sky.
The packet fell from Neiyu's hand. Beneath it, cold metal caught the light. More of it lay packed tightly together, deep under the food.
They were already too late.
BOOM!
A deafening blast erupted deep in the warehouse. High-explosive shells, incendiary rounds, and stacks of compressed food went up together. Fire and the shock wave tore the building apart in an instant. A column of flame rose as if it would set the whole sky alight.
Something slammed into Neiyu from behind. Every sound cut out. All she could feel was her teacher gripping her hand and the tremendous shove coming from her direction. Her teacher had put herself between Neiyu and the blast.
Neiyu's vision dimmed. The last thing she saw before she lost consciousness was her teacher's wings on fire.
Flames climbed the white feathers. They burned and burned…
…………
When Neiyu opened her eyes again, she saw an unfamiliar ceiling. Then she noticed the Milira rushing about around her. She caught snatches of conversation and slowly pieced together what had happened.
The attack had been planned for the Milira. The humans knew they were short of food. They'd prepared decoy warehouses and leaked their locations through different channels. They meant to lure in the Milira and kill them with the high-explosive and incendiary shells hidden inside.
No one knew where those munitions came from. Whoever had sold the weapons had probably already left the rimworld aboard a ship.
Something struck Neiyu and she whipped her head around. “Where's my teacher?”
No one answered. “Where's my teacher?!”
The Milira tending to her said nothing and slowly looked to the other side.
Neiyu followed her gaze. Her teacher lay in the next bed. Her halo had shattered. Most of her white wings had burned away, and what remained couldn't be saved.
She'd lost both legs and the arm she'd held out to shield Neiyu from the blast. Severe burns covered her body. She was alive, asleep and still.
“Teacher…” Neiyu stared at her.
“Teacher!” She tried to climb out of bed and only then realized that she, too, was covered in bandages. The pain sent her falling back.
“Why…” Neiyu's voice began to shake. She looked at her teacher and thought of the humans she'd tied up. “I spared them… I did…”
She lowered her head. “Did I do something wrong?”
No one could answer her. Her teacher had already given her an answer.
We were the invaders this time. We came to take their food.
They were protecting themselves, too. They set their traps and fought back the way they could.
Even if they hated us, even if we hated them… we just stood on different sides.
——————————
The tune on the roof stopped. Neiyu looked down at the colony again. The man she'd once struck down now lived here, and he was carrying freshly harvested grain along the road. When he saw her on the eaves, he still looked away without thinking.
Neiyu didn't say a word. She just stroked the flower in her hand. A long time passed before she seemed to understand something at last.
LanguageData.MX_Biography_Neiyu.stories.3.storyText:
The feeling welling up inside her could no longer be held back—
“Go. Take your companions with you into deep space.”
The same voice rose out of the chaos within her, repeating itself until it filled her mind.
After her teacher was confined to a wheelchair, Neiyu gave nearly everything she had to her people's war. She returned to the battlefield, was wounded, and came back alive through blood and fire, over and over.
Fighting tempered her body and hardened her resolve. She was no longer the child who'd hidden behind her teacher the first time she picked up the blade. Many of her kin saw her as a warrior who could stand on her own.
It was then that Neiyu killed the arms dealers hiding aboard a ship in deep space. They had never imagined a Milira could fly clear of the atmosphere and reach their ship in orbit. The shock was still plain on their faces when she stood before them.
On that ship, Neiyu found a report that made her furious. “The Empire… the so-called glitterworlds.” She whispered the words as the papers crumpled in her hand.
What the report described was simple enough to make her sick. The heirs of powerful families each chose a faction on the rimworld to back. Guns, ammunition, medicine, technology, supplies. They bankrolled their chosen sides and made bets, staking a planet and the future of everything alive on it for a little amusement.
The entire sector was sealed off. It was hard to enter and harder to leave. They watched their chosen factions grow, watched cities fall and whole peoples die, watched one war after another drag the planet into ruin.
When one side finally won, the winners collected their chips and the game was over. After that, there was no reason for anyone to pay attention to the planet.
Cut off from their sponsors' technology, supplies, and weapons, the local factions they'd propped up often couldn't keep going as they had. Some civilizations struggled on in the ruins. Some descended into years of civil war. Others gradually fell back on the most basic means of survival. None of those futures looked bright.
All because the people “above” wanted some entertainment. What was a life worth to someone who could shrug at the loss of a planet?
At first the Milira hardly caught their attention. They were just one more people native to the rimworld. That changed as more outsiders took notice of their appearance and unusual bodies.
No one knew how many Milira had been taken, loaded onto ships, and carried into deep space to the so-called glitterworlds.
“Go. Take your companions with you into deep space.”
The voice sounded again. Neiyu rubbed her eyes. She was sitting on the bridge of the transport the Milira had captured. The low hum of running equipment was the only sound.
“What do we need?” Neiyu whispered. “Why do we have to go through this?”
No one answered. “What if we're not tough enough? What if we can't grow any stronger? What if next time they bring more than guns and bombs?”
Neiyu slowly lowered her head. “What will we have to rely on then?”
——————————
Soon after, Neiyu shared what she'd learned with the surviving Milira. Many of them gathered to hear her that day.
Neiyu stood before them. Her teacher sat below, the marks of her burns still visible, watching her student quietly from her wheelchair.
“We Milira have bodies far tougher than most. We can fly and use powers other peoples scarcely understand. From birth, we're stronger than most living beings.”
Neiyu paused and looked out at her kin. “I still don't think that's enough.”
A murmur went through the crowd. Neiyu went on. “We need to grow stronger. We have to be strong enough that no one can stand above us and decide what happens to us on a whim.”
She clenched her fist. “We have to be strong enough to crush anyone who tries to dictate our fate. We survived on this planet by our own strength once. Why can't we keep going that way?”
Someone in the crowd interrupted her. An older Milira lifted her head to look up at Neiyu.
“Because we're already strong. There's little on this planet that could kill one of us with its bare hands.”
She didn't raise her voice, but the people around her fell quiet. “It's the weapons humans make that kill us. The blast at the granary injured your teacher and dozens of our kin. We can't dismiss technology after that. Their shells are already closing the gap between us and everyone else.”
Another Milira stood. “We're quick learners. Why shouldn't we develop technology of our own? We have strong bodies and the minds to learn. We could have both strength and technology. That's the future we should work toward.”
More of their kin agreed. The Milira were proud. They doubted an ordinary person could physically surpass them. Yet the last few years had made one thing clear to more and more of them: they lacked the technology to stand up to the powers beyond their sky.
“And why are you so sure we can get much stronger?” someone else asked Neiyu. “We can't improve overnight. Even with our long lives, it takes decades to strengthen the body. A century, sometimes. How much stronger could we possibly get?”
“We can train all we like. Can we cause an explosion that reaches for kilometers with our bodies alone? Kill hundreds of thousands with a single blow? Cross the stars on a pair of wings?” The Milira held her gaze. “Why should we stake our future on that?”
More eyes settled on Neiyu. Some were uncertain, some openly skeptical, some contemptuous.
Neiyu said nothing and slowly closed her eyes. The voice returned, clearer than she'd ever heard it before.
“Come to deep space. Come to me. I can set you on the path to ascension. I can give each of you… greater power.”
“Come… come.”
Neiyu opened her eyes and looked past the crowd. In the distance, the transport the Milira had captured stood waiting.
The ship could pilot itself. Give it a set of coordinates and it would plot a course and carry everyone aboard to that sector.
Most Milira didn't want to leave. They knew this land. They'd been born here, grown up here, fought here. It was their home.
But if they stayed forever, how could they stand against the glitterworlds beyond their sky? How could they ever fight back?
"The transport," Neiyu said suddenly.
The room fell quiet. She lifted her head. "We have a transport ship."
She paused, then decided to lie. "I found a report aboard it. It said that somewhere in deep space there's a way for living beings to become much more powerful."
The room erupted. Some asked her for proof, others waited to see her make a fool of herself. Neiyu continued. "I think we should go. At the very least, we should see for ourselves whether that power exists."
Only she knew there was no report. All of it had come from that voice deep within her. She knew neither where the presence came from nor what it wanted. But the future it described... she did want to believe in it.
Neiyu had never been one to trust in things outside herself. Weapons could be destroyed, cities taken, technology left behind. Even the finest equipment might wind up as scrap. Power that belonged to her alone would be harder to take away.
If she could stand on her own against whatever enemy came for her, would what happened to her teacher ever have to happen again? Would anyone else be driven from home by a war? The real enemy might not even have bothered to pay attention to them.
“Is he really right? Is he?” Neiyu kept asking herself. She'd never stopped being wary of that voice. Nothing comes free. Why would someone she'd never even met offer her people that kind of strength?
Yet before the voice came, she'd already been lost. She had no answers and no clear way forward. Even if this road was dangerous, she wanted to see where it went.
“It's worth trying. Even if it takes everything we have, even if it takes our whole lives, we can't let the chance go.”
Neiyu looked out at her kin again. “I'm going aboard that ship. I don't know if anyone wants to come with me. I don't know where it will lead or whether we'll find what I think we will.”
Neiyu stepped forward. “But I'm willing to go.”
She didn't speak loudly, but everyone could hear her. “I'm willing to try. If we really can reach that place and gain enough strength to protect ourselves and our home, then someone ought to try.”
Neiyu raised her head. “I believe that.”
The crowd went quiet. At length, one Milira rose. Then another, and a third, and a fourth.
More and more rose. Some were fighters fresh from battle, their wings still scarred. Some had barely reached adulthood and had never left the settlement. Neiyu saw something of herself in their eyes, though they were still only a small part of her people.
The first young Milira looked up at Neiyu. “We're willing to try.”
She looked around at the others still seated. “I think you're right, too. It makes sense to stay, learn from the humans, and build our own cities.”
She paused. “But if there is another way, we should have the courage to look at it, even if we don't know where it leads.”
The crowd fell quiet again. Neiyu waited, watching the young woman. Then more people stood.
Some still hesitated. One looked back at her family, another toward the battered settlement. Others looked down, weighing what it would mean to go.
This would be no ordinary migration or brief voyage. No one knew where the transport would take them, or whether ascension or death awaited them in deep space.
Neiyu took a breath. “I won't ask anyone to follow me. You can stay. You can study what the humans left behind, repair our settlement, and build our own cities. And you can wait for us to come home.”
Neiyu looked up. The sky was still dim. The great transport waited in the distance, its hull blackened and pocked with bullet scars. Beneath that rimworld sky it looked like a steel beast crouched against the ground.
“But someone has to go. Someone has to see for herself how high that sky above us really goes.”
Neiyu slowly closed her hand into a fist. “Someone has to find out what gives those people from the glitterworlds the right to stake a planet, a civilization, and countless lives at a gambling table.”
She lifted her head. “If they can stand up there and look down at us, one day we should be able to stand where they do and look them in the eye.”
There were no cheers or applause. More and more Milira simply stood in silence. It was a weightier answer than any cheer.
Neiyu's teacher watched from her wheelchair. The fire had left marks that would never wholly fade. Her once-white wings were still ragged, broad patches of dark red burns visible on her bare skin. Her expression was calm.
Once the crowd began to disperse, her teacher lifted a hand. “Little Yu.”
Neiyu stopped and turned. “Teacher.”
Her teacher looked at her. “You lied.”
Neiyu stiffened.
“There was no report like that on the transport. Was there?”
Neiyu was quiet a long time. At last she nodded. “…No.”
Her teacher didn't scold her. She just asked, “Why do you still want to go?”
Neiyu lowered her head. “Because… I heard a voice.”
She spoke softly. “It started calling to me a long time ago. It knew about us and what was happening here. It said there was a path in deep space meant for us.”
Her teacher watched her. “Do you believe it?”
“I don't know.” Neiyu shook her head. “That's why I'm going. If he's lying, I want to see for myself what he wants from us. But if he's telling the truth…”
Neiyu looked back. The Milira who had decided to leave were already gathering supplies in the distance. “I can't let this chance slip away.”
Her teacher laughed. “You were the same as a child. Scared half to death, always running straight into the worst of it.”
Neiyu didn't argue. Her teacher slowly reached out. Neiyu crouched so the scarred hand could settle on her head.
“Then go. See what's out there. See what this power you've been chasing really is.”
Her teacher paused. “Little Yu.”
Neiyu looked up.
“Power has never been the answer. It gives you the right to choose one.”
Neiyu went still. Her teacher met her eyes. “Remember why you want to grow stronger. If you ever grow so strong that no one can force your hand, remember what you set out to protect.”
Neiyu was quiet for a moment, then nodded solemnly. “I will.”
——————————
The list of those leaving kept growing. At first there were barely a dozen. Then more than twenty, then more than thirty.
Within a few days, some who'd strongly opposed leaving had changed their minds. They didn't necessarily believe the report was real or that ascension awaited them in deep space. With the ship already in their hands, they felt someone ought to see what lay outside the sector.
In the end there were ninety-nine names on the list. Ninety-nine Milira. A handful next to their whole people.
No one knew then that those ninety-nine names would mark the beginning of another age.
——————————
There was no great ceremony on the day they left. The transport started up slowly. Its enormous engines whipped up wind across the plain, lifting dust and buffeting the Milira's wings.
Those staying behind stood far back. Some watched in silence. Some waved. A few still thought they were embarking on a pointless adventure.
Neiyu paused at the foot of the gangway and looked back one last time. Her teacher sat at the front of the crowd, in the same wheelchair. She didn't wave. She just watched Neiyu from afar.
Neiyu said nothing, either. She put a hand to her chest, bowed deeply, and went aboard.
The heavy hatch slowly closed, shutting out the wind and the voices outside.
The ninety-nine Milira spread across the bridge and the cargo bay, quietly watching the equipment light up around them. Many had never been inside anything that large.
The hull began to vibrate. A cold, mechanical voice came from the navigation system. “Destination confirmed. Coordinates locked. Deep-space course plotted.”
Neiyu sat in the center of the bridge. On the star chart before her, a course led away from their rimworld and into a region of deep space none of them knew.
“Come…” The voice came again, clearer than ever.
“Come. Leave that narrow sky behind. Come to me, and I'll show you how far life can reach.”
Neiyu closed her eyes and gave no answer. A moment later, she opened them and looked out at the endless stars. “Begin.”
The transport's engines roared. The great steel ship lifted free of the ground. The land fell away. Cities shrank, mountains flattened into a faint line, and finally the whole planet hung quiet beyond the window, suspended in darkness.
The transport kept climbing and left the atmosphere behind. For the first time, stars filled their view without anything in between.
No one on the bridge spoke. Standing there, they realized how small everything they'd known seemed against the stars: their wars, their home, their hatred, their dead, even the visitors from the glitterworlds who had once loomed over them.
Neiyu watched the stars. As a child she'd looked up at these same lights and thought they were little points hung in the sky. Now she was flying toward them.
“Will we ever come back?” a Milira beside her asked.
Neiyu looked through the window. Their home was slowly receding. It was a long time before she spoke. “Yes. Once we have the strength to decide our own fate, we'll come back.”
The transport accelerated. Their homeworld faded into the darkness. Ahead of them lay a course no one had taken before.
Ninety-nine Milira left their home. No one knew what lives, worlds, or powers awaited them out there in deep space.
Only the voice from the chaos still whispered to Neiyu. “Come. A little closer. Your path has barely begun.”
The transport disappeared among the stars. A new age began for the Milira.
LanguageData.MX_Biography_Neiyu.stories.4.storyText:
“Mm-hm… about me.” Neiyu drew out the last word. Someone wanted to know where the fragment sitting before them had come from. She tilted her head in thought, gathered her clothes, and sat cross-legged.
“There's too much to tell before that. We spent a long time drifting through deep space. Then the ship broke down and crashed on a planet none of us knew. After that we built houses, looked for food, fought, and tried to figure out all sorts of strange things…”
She counted a few off on her fingers and gave up with a wave. “Oh, I'll tell those stories another time. If I started at the beginning, we'd be here till tomorrow.”
Neiyu smiled, but the smile soon faded. “Let's start with the day I became immortal. From that day on, there wasn't a soul left in the world who remembered me.” She was still smiling as she tapped her fingertips twice against her knee.
——
The day of her ascension came 230 years after the Day of Rebirth.
Neiyu spent a long time getting dressed that morning. She straightened her collar, cuffs, and belt, then smoothed the stray feathers on her wings one by one. Muhe had given her a bright green leaf pendant and tied it at her waist herself.
“A lot of people are going to be watching you today. You can't be the first one to fly beyond Wupian and still look like you just woke up.”
Neiyu laughed at her fussing. After Muhe left, though, she tied two more knots in the pendant's cord. Three in all. When she was satisfied it wouldn't fall off, she nodded to herself.
The platform at the center of the settlement was surrounded, but only a small fraction of their people could be there in person. The rest watched from afar through communication spells. Their lights dotted mountains, forests, plains, and settlements.
Neiyu stood at the edge of the platform and closed her eyes. At Wupian, her senses could follow Ji through the world for hundreds and even thousands of li. She could make out what was happening far away as clearly as if it were beside her.
In a snowy northern valley, a spirit beast broke through the thin new ice on a river. Far out at sea, waves struck dark reefs and swept away footprints that hadn't yet dried along the shore. In a settlement farther away still, a young Milira had just completed First Listening. She felt Ji flowing for the first time, but couldn't yet sustain even the simplest circulation.
Two hundred and thirty years had passed. The ninety-nine Milira who had left their home were now the oldest of their people. Settlements stood where there had been wasteland, a new generation had been born, and roads ran between them. The Milira had rebuilt their civilization on this strange planet. They'd even found a name for the power that had once baffled them: Ji.
First Listening, Feather Setting, Crown Setting, Sigil Inscription, Pattern Formation, Resonant Halo, Return to Ji, and Wupian. Over two centuries, the methods for reaching all eight stages had been refined, written down and taught to the Milira who came after. Today, Neiyu would try to go beyond the last of them.
Cheers rang out across the settlements, mingled with calls of her name and prayers for her safety. Some were already debating what to call the next stage. Godhood, immortality, a feathered immortal, or a name no one had ever spoken?
Neiyu opened her eyes, but there was little relief on her face. For years, one question had bothered her. Why had her cultivation gone so smoothly?
When she first sensed Ji, she hadn't had time to think before the way to feel it came to her. Before Feather Setting, she dreamed of pinpoints of light beginning at the roots of her feathers, following their channels through her bones and into her body, then returning to the world around her. The following day she tried it, and it worked.
The same thing happened with Crown Setting, Sigil Inscription, Pattern Formation and Resonant Halo. Every time she reached the end of a stage, the next method came to her just in time to carry on. No one had gone farther, and no one could have taught her. It all seemed to come from her own reasoning. But when she tried to recall how she'd worked any of it out, there was nothing. The conclusions were clear. How she'd reached them was a blank.
The presence never hurried her. It no longer even whispered in her ear as it had long ago.
She could have refused. But the Milira who had lived through the Day of Rebirth couldn't afford to wait.
Most of their technology had been left behind. The transport that carried ninety-nine Milira through deep space was nearly destroyed in the crash. The sky, the ground, and the creatures on this planet were all unfamiliar. Some spirit beasts could tear a Milira apart with ease. The strength they'd once taken pride in was barely enough to keep them alive.
First Listening let them sense Ji. Feather Setting strengthened their bodies and wings. Each stage that followed kept more of them alive, and settlements rose where they hadn't been able to set foot before. By the time Neiyu began asking where those answers really came from, far more than her ninety-eight companions depended on her. Her whole people cultivated using the methods she'd passed on. She couldn't stop now, but she was growing more afraid of what would happen if she kept going.
“Yu, what's on your mind?”
A tap on the shoulder brought Neiyu back. Muhe had come up beside her, her green eyes creased in a smile. A few blades of grass growing between the stones bent gently toward her.
Muhe leaned closer and studied Neiyu's face. "You don't look like someone about to become immortal."
"Oh, come on. What am I supposed to look like?"
"Like this, obviously." Muhe straightened her back, lifted her chin and put on a solemn face. "Today I, Neiyu, ascend to immortality. Henceforth, in heaven and on earth, I alone..."
She laughed before she could finish. Neiyu laughed too, then her face slowly went still.
"He."
"Hm?"
Neiyu looked into the distance. "It's just a what-if. What if I've been wrong all along?"
"We believe in you. We've followed you this far, and you're still worrying about that?"
"But..."
Muhe turned to her. "Why so many questions today?"
Neiyu didn't answer. Muhe watched her for a moment, dropped the joke, and came closer to straighten the crooked leaf pendant at her waist.
"Yu, we just want you to be safe. Become a god, become immortal, fly up there and find nothing beyond Wupian. No one will blame you." She stepped back and smiled again. "Just don't forget us."
Neiyu touched the pendant. "What if I really do forget?"
“Then we'll get to know each other all over again. Meet me today, meet the others tomorrow.” Muhe lifted her chin. “If there's one thing we Milira have, isn't it time?”
Neiyu looked at her and nearly let all her doubts spill out. The methods her people had practiced for more than two centuries might never have been hers. Something really might be waiting for her beyond Wupian.
Her whole people had been waiting for this day. What would happen if she told them now that an unknown presence might have shaped the practice from the very start? Two centuries of cultivation, and all the work, fighting, healing, and daily life that depended on Ji, would be affected. She had no proof. She couldn't throw away a path that had saved so many lives on the strength of a feeling.
She wanted to see for herself what lay beyond Wupian.
Muhe turned away, her face growing solemn. Green light spread from the edge of her halo and joined the settlement's communication spells. The waiting Milira fell silent, and Ji carried her voice across the land.
“Hear this, Milira in every land. For two hundred and thirty years, Neiyu has carried our forebears' legacy and kept our people safe. She has mastered every stage from First Listening to Wupian. Today she rises to the heavens and knocks at their gate. She seeks a way to immortality, so those who come after her may have a path to follow.”
Neiyu stood behind her and listened.
“Let us pray as one. May her wings find their way home. May her path carry her to its end. May our forebears watch over all living things. May we stand by one another and keep the flame alive.”
Muhe lifted her head. “May we, the Milira, endure through all the ages.”
Millions of halos lit up, from cities and fields in the mountains to the forests, snowfields, and islands. Neiyu let out a breath.
“Here I go, then.”
Muhe nodded. “Go.”
The Ji Neiyu had gathered over the years poured out of her with a low hum. Light spread over her wings until it reached every feather. The platform trembled. Dust and bits of stone lifted, and points of light appeared in the air.
Neiyu rose. Several Milira who had also reached Wupian spread their wings and followed, forming a wide circle below her. They were her escort, and if she failed, they would be there to catch her.
The air still held the warmth of the ground at first. Above the clouds the cold cut to the bone. Neiyu flew on, leaving the storm beneath her and the sounds of the ground fading away. She stopped and lifted her eyes to the familiar stars. There was nothing between her and them now.
Neiyu closed her eyes. “Let's begin.”
Ji flowed through her. The Resonant Halo trembled, her feather channels opened, and the marks formed during Sigil Inscription lit one by one. The laws of life, death, matter, psychic power, time, and space showed on her body.
Ji began gathering around her, first from hundreds of li away, then thousands, then farther still. It went just as she'd calculated, right up to the moment the first thread of Ji crossed the boundary of Wupian.
Neiyu opened her eyes. Unfamiliar knowledge appeared in her mind once again. She had no idea where it came from or how it had been worked out, yet it was so clear and complete she couldn't help believing it was right. There were only three characters in the name of the next stage: the immortal Neiyu.
The earlier stages had been named for states of cultivation. This one bore her name. She felt no joy. The name had come with the price of reaching it.
Her body, her wings, her halo, her consciousness, her memories.
Neiyu's pupils narrowed.
Her name, her ties of cause and consequence, her connections, every trace she'd left.
She stopped breathing for an instant. It would cost her everything. She could keep her life and soul, but even the fact that she had once existed would have to go.
“No…”
Neiyu snapped her wings shut and stopped the Ji flowing through her, trying to break off the ascension. The power outside her gathered faster. She forced the Resonant Halo still, but the shock almost made her lose control of Ji. She sealed her feather channels, cut off the sigils, reversed Return to Ji, and even tried to shatter the state she'd achieved at Wupian.
Every attempt moved the ritual forward. From First Listening onward, everything she had learned was part of it. However she used it, she couldn't bring the ritual to a stop.
First Listening had let her hear Ji. Feather Setting had let her carry more of it. Every later stage had refined her all the way to Wupian. She had thought she'd reached the end of her cultivation. What she'd finished was an offering fit for sacrifice.
Neiyu went cold. Before leaving home, she'd sat on the captured transport and heard a voice calling to her again and again.
“Come to deep space. Come to me. I can set you on the path to ascension.”
Two hundred and thirty years later, he'd kept his promise. The Milira had gained power, and she'd reached the threshold of ascension. He hadn't lied. Only now did she know what ascension would cost her.
The stars were silent. No gates opened and nothing divine descended. Something opened its “eyes” through the Ji in her. She couldn't comprehend its shape, tell how far away it was, or even be sure it existed in the same universe. She couldn't call what she felt a gaze. She only knew it had noticed her.
“Get out of here! All of you!”
Neiyu shouted to her escort, but the sudden blaze of light swallowed her voice. Below the clouds, the Milira could only see the Ji around her growing clearer and vaster, approaching a state they couldn't grasp. They backed away as planned to give her room.
“Did it work?” someone asked.
“Almost, I think. She's already gone well beyond Wupian.”
Another Milira looked up. “Nei…” She stopped halfway through the name.
“Hm? What is it?”
“Her. The one up there…” The Milira frowned. “What was her name again?”
The woman beside her blinked. The same bewilderment crossed her face.
Neiyu heard them clearly up there. The chill that crept into her mind was sharper than the feeling of her body being torn apart. They'd forgotten her name. Then they forgot her voice.
The cheers below came slowly to a stop. Some Milira kept looking up and couldn't remember why they'd gathered. Others remembered someone was trying to get beyond Wupian, but couldn't say who she was or why they'd waited so solemnly for her.
Neiyu realized her face had disappeared from their memories. The room she'd lived in remained, but it had never had an occupant. All the things on her desk had new histories. Every volume of her cultivation notes was still there, every word intact, with a blank space where her name had been.
Other people had called the meetings she used to lead. Decisions she'd made were now decisions everyone had made together. The Milira she'd rescued remembered the spirit beast and remembered surviving. All they'd forgotten was who had stood between them and it. Their memories filled in the gaps on their own, and no one thought anything was amiss.
Neiyu looked down for Muhe. She was still below the clouds, green eyes fixed on the sky.
"He..."
Muhe seemed to hear and looked up. But the recognition in her eyes was fading, and her brow drew tighter and tighter. The figure in the sky was clearly someone important. Watching her disappear made Muhe's chest ache. She couldn't even say who she was, much less why it hurt.
Neiyu opened her mouth to call down again. She wanted to say she was Neiyu, little Yu, the one who'd run through the wilderness with Muhe for more than two hundred years. She was still wearing the pendant Muhe had tied on her.
She stopped with the words in her throat. Everything they'd shared was being stripped away. Even if she told her, Muhe wouldn't be able to keep the memory.
Below was the land where her people had lived for 230 years. The practice from First Listening to Wupian would survive, and the one who had started it would vanish. In a hundred years, two hundred, a thousand, some other Milira would reach Wupian and find those three characters. She would be the next offering. Who would be left to tell her what had happened here?
Neiyu wasn't especially afraid to die. Thinking of her people following her into the same trap, she began struggling again to leave them a warning.
“At least… at least let me leave this!”
She shaped Ji into words. They vanished as soon as they took shape. She tried setting a memory into the pattern of the laws, then carving the warning into the Ji of the world itself. Neither held. The power erased every trace of her, even the words she'd just written.
The light around her grew brighter. Her body came apart, her wings turned to dust from the tips inward, and her halo cracked. Her thoughts blurred. The few ties she still had to the world were about to break.
All at once it felt unfair. When they left home, she'd promised to go back as soon as they were strong enough to decide their own fate. She'd come this far and still hadn't gone back.
Her teacher must have been gone a long time. She didn't know what home looked like now. There was so much left unfinished, so much she hadn't said.
Neiyu lowered her head, and a tear fell. It slipped through her fading cheek instead of dissolving in the light. The clouds and the wind couldn't stop it, and even the forgetting closing in around her couldn't erase it.
She watched the tear fall farther away. Perhaps that was the last thing she still had to give.
The tear landed on Muhe's face. She touched something cool and wet and felt a sudden ache in her chest she couldn't explain. She looked up sharply and saw only a white light too bright to look at.
“Who… who was just…?”
Halfway through the question, she forgot what she meant to ask.
The white light folded in on itself. Neiyu's body, wings, and halo vanished. There was no body, no remnant, nothing to carry home. No one cried for her.
Ji poured out of the sky into mountains, forests, wastelands, and oceans, reaching down into canyons and deep underground. Even places where there had barely been any Ji filled up. Its concentration rose sharply across the entire planet.
After a brief silence, cheers broke out everywhere.
“The Ji concentration went up!”
“What happened?”
“Some kind of omen?”
“Write it down!”
“Get a reading, quick!”
The Milira felt Ji flowing thicker than ever. Some thought a new age was coming. Others guessed there must be a stage beyond Wupian no one had discovered. No one asked where Neiyu had gone. They no longer remembered that there'd ever been a Milira by that name.
The escorts landed and gathered around Muhe to ask what to do next. She hesitated, then took charge as if it were the natural thing to do. In everyone's memory, she'd always been the one who'd led them through the days after Rebirth, founded their settlements, and developed the cultivation that had brought them this far.
“Muhe, why are you crying?” one of her kin asked.
“Am I?” Muhe touched her face. Her fingers were wet. That hollow feeling came back again, as if she'd lost something. She couldn't think of what it could have been. “I don't know,” she said softly.
She couldn't bring herself to wipe the tear away or let it fall. Green light rose from her fingertips. A little shoot grew from her palm, opened its leaves, flowered, and formed a green seedpod no bigger than her fingernail. She sealed the tear inside it and held it tight.
“I can't lose this.”
Her companion looked more puzzled. “Why?”
Muhe was quiet for a long time. All she could say was, “I don't know.”
By the time she looked up again, the white light had faded. The clouds were drawing together, and sunlight fell through the gaps.
——
Neiyu stopped there. She looked down and turned the faint leaf-shaped pendant at her waist between her fingers, rubbing its edge again and again. A long time passed before she looked up with a smile.
"And after that, I was gone." She spread her hands. "Poof. Nothing left."
"She didn't remember me at all. But she still had that tear." Neiyu blinked, a little mischief in her smile. "Maybe she hadn't forgotten me completely."
She looked down at her hands and fell quiet for a while.
"Lucky for me, I did have a few things to fall back on..."
She lifted her head, smiling. "Anyway, that's how I became immortal." She paused and added softly, "That was the first time the immortal Neiyu came into being."
LanguageData.MX_Biography_Neiyu.stories.5.storyText:
"The first time?" the person beside her asked as soon as she finished. "Does that mean there'll be a second?"
"Sure," she said at once, then thought for a moment. "That's the plan, anyway. When? Not for a long while yet."
The Raiment Blossom at her collar was blooming as brightly as ever. If you hadn't heard it from her own lips, it would've been hard to connect this Milira who wandered about all day with the ascension she'd just described.
"But you've already been burned once."
"All the more reason not to rush this time." Neiyu tucked the pendant back into the folds of her clothes and took out the little notebook she always carried. The added pages had warped the spine. She had to hold it open with her hand to keep it from snapping shut.
Someone recognized a page about the colony's last harvest. Neiyu had worked in the fields all day. Come supper, the cook had chased her out of the kitchen for meddling with the grill. She'd written it down, then crossed out the lines about the grill.
“What does that have to do with becoming immortal?”
Neiyu followed their gaze and turned the page. “Ask me anything else. I'm not telling that one.” She held the notebook close and let them finish laughing. “But these things do matter. I'm still here partly because of something I did to prepare.”
“You knew something would go wrong?”
“I knew the voice wanted me to do something. He brought us all that way and taught me so much. He couldn't have done it just to hear me say thanks. At the time, I didn't know what he really wanted.”
Neiyu shut the notebook, keeping her thumb where she'd opened it. "I thought of plenty of things that could go wrong. When the day came, I found it still wasn't enough."
——
It was long before her ascension when Neiyu first made serious plans for a way back.
That night she sat at her desk until dawn, with several pages on Resonant Halo spread in front of her. She'd already tried the method written there. It worked. But as she followed her notes and worked it out all over again, she came to a point where she couldn't connect what happened before with what came after.
Neiyu took a fresh sheet and circled the gap on the old one. In the past, she'd have followed the method in her head and left whatever she didn't understand for later. The desk was already piled with papers like this. Some she'd written years earlier.
She stopped and wrote on another sheet: Why did he want me to learn all this?
The voice gave her no answer. She waited a little longer, folded the paper, and put it in the bottom drawer.
At dawn she went out as usual. The new clinic was trying out the circulation method she'd taught. A woman with an injured feather channel could already get out of bed. Hearing Neiyu come in, she tried to push herself upright. Neiyu eased her back down, examined the injury, and left instructions for what to adjust. It wasn't until she walked out that she thought of the paper in the drawer again.
Those methods really had saved people. She couldn't ask everyone to abandon what they'd learned or conjure another viable path from a suspicion. She had to keep studying and work out what could still be done if it all went wrong.
She began by putting her notes in order, marking which ideas she'd tested herself and which were still guesses. She sent copies to different settlements and asked a few Milira familiar with the methods to repeat the work on their own. Where they couldn't explain a result, they wrote down the question. Whoever found something new would send it around for the others to check.
She stopped keeping all the originals in her room. Once, Muhe came by, saw a large patch of bare desk, and thought Neiyu had finally tidied up.
“I gave them away,” Neiyu said. “If they can't find me someday, they'll be able to keep going.”
Muhe leafed through the pages that were left. “Good. Maybe every time you go out they won't come to me asking when you'll be back.”
Neiyu laughed. Once Muhe set the papers down, Neiyu made another copy of the unanswered questions and tucked it into her own set.
She dug up the old transport's star charts, too. With the few who still studied its navigation equipment, she checked records that had gone unused for years and talked through how to preserve the supplies and technology for another voyage. Someone asked whether she meant to go home. She answered in earnest: if they could go back, they'd better make sure the route was still there.
She had no idea how much their home had changed. She only remembered what she'd said before she boarded. She didn't want to find out what they needed to get back on the day they were finally able to leave.
The work took a long time. The settlements grew, and there was less and less that had to wait for her return. Neiyu felt easier every time she saw someone else take over. When she cultivated alone, though, she still felt as if something were guiding her.
Her people could carry on the work and were preparing for another voyage. What if she was the one something happened to?
She tried writing down things only she would know and sealing the sheets away. She also tried storing memories in Ji, then retrieving them after a while to check them against her own. The records held up well, with hardly even small errors. Every time she checked, she still felt something was missing.
One memory held the day her teacher showed her how to grip a blade. She could see exactly where she'd put her fingers wrong, hear her teacher correcting her, even remember how long that blade had seemed. The record could only play that day back. She asked a question she'd thought of years later. The teacher in it went on showing her how to hold the blade, and little Neiyu nodded just as she had before.
Neiyu put the memory away again. She still wanted to see it, but she couldn't count on it to make decisions if something happened to her. She began trying to separate a small part of her own consciousness.
There was no method she could follow. She began with what she knew of the laws and her own mind, trying a little at a time. Sometimes all she separated were a few stray thoughts that never answered her. Sometimes a fragment held together until it moved a little farther away, then dissolved back into Ji.
After the worst attempt, Neiyu sat on the floor for a long time. She clearly remembered what she'd done and knew how to draw the power back in. She just couldn't bring herself to care about anything happening around her. Someone called from outside. She heard them and recognized the voice, but it took her a while to think of answering.
She stopped for days. Only when she opened her old notes and found herself annoyed by her own mistakes did she start again.
She separated less of herself each time and stopped rushing to give the fragments power. How much they could remember and how long they could last would take time to learn. At first they were very faint and for the most part had to use her senses to see the world beyond her.
During one attempt, as she concentrated on keeping a fragment together, her gaze drifted to the window. Under the eaves a bird was tugging at a stalk of grass. It caught the stalk in its beak again and again but couldn't pull it free of the crack.
Neiyu hadn't paid it any mind. The fragment watched intently and didn't settle down until the bird pulled the stalk free and flew off.
After a moment, she asked in her head, “What were you looking at?”
Her own voice came back to her. “Where is it building its nest?”
Neiyu looked outside. The roof hid the treetop, and she couldn't see where the bird had gone. She stepped out, rounded the corner, and with the fragment found the nest hidden among the branches.
Once she came back in, she sat over her notes for a long time before writing. She hadn't planned any of that. That little piece of her mind could pay attention on its own and grow curious about things she'd never noticed.
More attempts still failed, but Neiyu finally understood what she wanted to keep. She separated more fragments and got them to hold together on their own. Each carried only some of her memories and strength. None could be a whole Neiyu yet, but she didn't need them to do everything for her.
If she were trapped, at least part of her could try to leave. If someone tampered with her judgment, a fragment they hadn't touched might realize something was wrong. She couldn't know which preparation would work. She could just try to keep a single failure from ruining them all.
Most of the fragments slept. Neiyu kept them apart from her everyday thoughts and checked one by one that they could wake and keep themselves together. She didn't send them away yet. She wasn't strong enough to keep them active for long on distant worlds, and she couldn't tell whether that voice would still be able to reach them, even apart from her.
She left a way to separate them later and tested how to wake them if she was harmed. Her first instructions for what to do next were very detailed.
Return to the settlement, find someone you trust, and check on the original. If she can't be saved, take over the work she left unfinished. She wrote a whole page and kept going, right down to some matters still pending in a few settlements.
She set down the pen and read it all again. If someone could distort her judgment, what made these instructions reliable? If the fragments did only what she'd written, something she hadn't foreseen could put them right back in the same trap.
She pulled the sheet out. She kept the specific details in a separate record they could refer to. The instructions she left them changed a great deal.
First, find a way to stay alive. Get help if you need it. If one thing doesn't work, try another. Leave this planet if you want. Go see somewhere else, or find somewhere to live. Even if the original is safe, those experiences are worth bringing home.
Neiyu thought about the bird and its nest. It had been a long time since she'd gone outside for a reason like that. There was always something to take care of when she opened her eyes, and cultivation took most of the time left. Sometimes she'd finish a retreat and find different people in nearby houses. She wouldn't even know where the old neighbors had gone.
She wanted the other selves to meet more people. There were places beyond home that she knew only as names on a star chart. There were things her teacher had told her long ago that she still hadn't sorted out for herself.
In the days before the ascension, Neiyu checked the sleeping fragments several more times. They carried little power. If something happened to her, none of them would be able to fix it straight away. As long as one could still act, however, the presence wouldn't get to decide everything.
It didn't put her at ease. No one could tell her whether she'd done enough when she didn't know what was coming. On the day of the ascension she thought again about telling Muhe what she feared. She couldn't get the words out. She flew up with a plan she'd never been able to put to the test.
——
“So you'd already split yourself up by then?”
“I'd prepared the parts I could split off,” Neiyu corrected. “Keeping them alive took a lot more work later. Some things I planned didn't help at all on the day.”
She looked down at the leaf pendant at her waist. “I left things people could use to check on me if I started acting strangely. Then they couldn't remember who I was. Who would they compare them with? I couldn't keep all the memories or the words, either. The tear that fell… I never expected that to survive.”
The room went quiet. Neiyu set the notebook on her knees. This time she didn't make a joke to change the subject.
“The story you saw ends with me disappearing. I hadn't quite died. There was a long way to go after that.”
Even now, much of what happened after ascension was hard to put into words. Her mortal body was gone, but her senses kept reaching outward. She could perceive things she'd never sensed at Wupian. With a thought she could turn aside a current of Ji that once would have taken all her strength to move. At the same time, her hold on who she was began to slip.
The past didn't simply vanish. Some memories were startlingly clear. She could remember a rainstorm a century earlier and name everyone who'd passed her in it, yet she was beginning to forget why she'd thought of them so often. She knew Muhe's name and remembered exactly how the pendant looked. The closeness she'd once felt when she said the name was growing harder to reach.
At first Neiyu thought the presence was doing all this to her. When she reached him at last, she realized that even he was fighting the same kind of erosion.
He'd ascended long ago. His own consciousness held power over higher laws, while the basic rules of the universe were steadily absorbing him. Neiyu had arrived there herself. Becoming immortal had made her part of the Heavenly Way. If it went on, the Neiyu who could be afraid and miss her home would disappear, and her will would go with her.
He hadn't expected Neiyu to appear there. As she tried to steady herself, his power bore down on her. She could feel him pushing her out and trying to wrest away the powers she'd only just touched. He saw what a threat she was and meant to stop her from growing any stronger.
Neiyu fought back. She held him off once but couldn't drive him away, and the assimilation continued. She had to fight on both fronts. The time had come to use what she'd prepared as a mortal.
She woke the sleeping fragments one at a time. Ascension had touched them, too. Some memories were already missing. Neiyu set aside enough of the power she could still command to hold them together, then changed her plan.
Bringing her old memories back would no longer be enough. She needed the fragments to live, to make their own choices about the people and things they met, and to grow through those experiences into a Neiyu with a whole self again. When they were ready to ascend once more, they could bring their experiences back, join the part of her still in the Heavenly Way, and try to stop the assimilation.
That was the chance she could still take. She couldn't prove it would work. She just knew she couldn't wait.
Neiyu used the Law of Space to send the fragments to worlds far apart. If things went wrong in one place, they might still have a chance somewhere else. Each place would be different. Each fragment would meet different people. Some would wake soon, others might take longer. What happened then would be up to them.
One of them found her way back to a rimworld.
Here there was none of the abundant Ji she'd known on that other planet. The fragment's power was limited, and there was no one waiting for her. When she asked about familiar names, there was no answer. When she said “Neiyu” to someone, they only repeated the unfamiliar name back to her.
She could still start a new life. She walked into the first settlement and told people her name. Then she went on to others. She kept a Raiment Blossom with her, sometimes letting it show her the way and finding a place to rest when she grew tired. Sometimes a promise kept her in one place a little longer. Sometimes she simply didn't want to leave.
Now she'd settled into life in this colony.
——
“So there are other versions of you out there?”
“Yes. I don't know where they are by now,” Neiyu said. “We've all seen different things since we split up. One of them might be a lot more diligent than I am and have done all sorts by now. Or she might be lazier than me and have found a nice place she never wants to leave.”
The person beside her pointed at the notebook on her knees. “So you write down what happens to everyone here because you want to take it all back with you?”
“I'll take it back. Writing it down is only a start.” Neiyu turned to a page and found something she'd written. “When this happened, I thought I understood it. It took a few more conversations with the person it happened to before I realized I'd got it wrong. I added these lines afterward.”
She'd made some changes on the page, and the last line was unfinished. She'd promised that person she would keep it private. She stopped reading and closed the book.
“There are still things I can't figure out. Say someone refuses to forgive you and you think there's still a way to make amends. Do you go back and find them? And the next time something like that happens somewhere else, the same answer might not fit.”
She looked out the door as she spoke. People in the colony were still at work. Voices came through the walls, too muffled to make out the words.
“I used to think that if I got strong enough, most things would sort themselves out. Now there are things I could help with, and I still need to hear what the other person actually wants first.”
“How much farther do you have to go before you can return?”
Neiyu thought for a while. “I don't know. I can't count it in pages. If I get as far as ascension again, I want to still know why these experiences matter and have a way of holding on to them. I haven't got there yet.”
“Won't you run into that thing all over again when you go back?”
“Yes.” This time she didn't hesitate. “The part of me that's still there is fighting him and waiting for the fragments to bring back a way out. I'll go back and help her when I'm ready.”
Neiyu put her hand on the notebook. “I learned later that he's an archotech that ascended through Ji, too. He wants to escape assimilation, but he won't share those powers with any other living being. Even if I find a way out for myself, he won't let me go easily, and he certainly won't let my people go any farther.”
“Once we can come back together, we still have to find a way to become immortal and stay ourselves. If it works, we'll leave the method for whoever comes after.” Her voice grew softer. “When my kin left home with me, they wanted a life worth living. I can't tell them in the end that they'll have to give up who they are to grow any stronger.”
The listener was silent for a moment. “What about us? When you take all this back, will you still remember this place?”
Neiyu looked down at the spine and smoothed a curling edge of paper with her hand.
“I want to.” She said, “When I get back and talk about this place, I still want to know why I liked living here, the way I know it now. If I can't do that, I haven't done what I set out to do.”
Someone called her to supper from the doorway. After a moment they added that she should keep out of the kitchen this time.
Neiyu called straight back, “I know!”
She put the notebook away, went to the door, and turned back to the person still sitting there. "By the way, did your family ever grow flowers like this?"
They nodded. "My mother did. They couldn't turn into bows or anything. We had to bring them indoors in winter."
"What were they called?"
"Let's eat first. I'll tell you in a bit."
